property_summary: After transferOwnership(newOwner) is called by the current owner, c.owner() must equal newOwner for every address; the mutant instead assigns msg.sender, so it violates this for any newOwner differing from the caller.

Rule: for any admissible newOwner (non-zero), after the owner successfully calls transferOwnership(newOwner), c.owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant never updates owner, so it breaks this for every input.

Ownership can only ever be changed by the current owner; since no owner is ever initialized, any call to transferOwnership from any caller must revert and leave owner unchanged (address(0)), but the mutant lets any caller set owner to an arbitrary non-zero address.
For any caller other than the current owner, transferOwnership leaves the owner unchanged; the mutant lets any caller set the owner to an arbitrary address.

A successful transferOwnership call must be made by the account that was owner immediately before the call (and a failed call must leave owner unchanged); the mutant lets any caller succeed, so for a non-zero caller the call succeeds although the prior owner differs.

For every non-owner caller, transferOwnership must revert and must not transfer ownership; the mutant runs the body before the check, so a non-owner caller who names himself as the new owner succeeds and takes ownership.

For any admissible actor, after ownership is transferred to that actor by the current owner, calling owned() from that actor must succeed; the mutated contract negates the onlyOwner check so it reverts for the owner and breaks this rule.
For every caller that is not the current owner, calling owned() must revert; the buggy contract removed the onlyOwner check, so a non-owner's call succeeds and owned() returns true.
For every non-owner address, calling owned() must revert (onlyOwner gates execution before the body); the mutant runs the body before the check, so a non-owner's call succeeds — violating the rule.
For every caller, owned() succeeds if and only if that caller is the current owner; the mutant runs the body before the ownership check, so a non-owner's call succeeds, violating the rule.

For every caller, calling owned() succeeds if and only if msg.sender equals the current owner, and a failed call must leave ownership untouched — the mutant runs the body before the ownership check so an ownership change by a would-be caller is attempted before reverting, breaking the rule for some input.
Since C's owner is initialized to address(0), for any non-zero caller the guarded transferOwnership must revert; the mutant inverts the check, so a non-owner caller succeeds and the rule is violated.

property_summary: Only the current owner may change ownership, so transferOwnership from a non-owner must revert and leave the owner unchanged; the mutant removed the require, so any caller succeeds and changes owner, breaking the rule for some fuzzed caller.

property_summary: For any newOwner supplied by an authorized caller, transferOwnership must set owner to exactly newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to address(this), which differs from newOwner for some inputs.
For any caller who is the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and sets c.owner() to newOwner; the mutant reverts on every call, so owner never changes.

For any actor, ownership may only be changed by the owner via transferOwnership; a call to owned() by the current owner must leave the publicly readable owner unchanged, which the mutant breaks by overwriting owner with msg.sender inside owned().

owned() must behave as a pure no-op for every caller: for any fuzzed address A, after ownership is (possibly) transferred to A by the owner, a subsequent call to owned() must leave the publicly readable c.owner() equal to A (and identical to what it was before the call); the mutant instead overwrites owner inside owned(), so any invocation path where the stored owner is not already msg.sender would expose the difference.

For any fuzzed addresses a and b (a != b), after the owner transfers ownership to a, calling owned() from a must be a storage no-op (owner stays a) and any call from a non-owner b must revert without changing owner; the mutant overwrites owner inside owned(), so a call by the current owner while a concurrent stake differs would expose the divergence — the assertion reads c.owner() and the revert flag of the boundary call.
